name: The sword in the stone: Whoso pulleth out this sword
scope: The boy Arthur draws the sword from the stone and is proclaimed king, from Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, Book I chapters 5-7 (Caxton 1485). T1: after the death of King UTHER PENDRAGON leaves BRITAIN without an heir, MERLIN the mage causes a great STONE to appear in a churchyard in LONDON on Christmas morning, and standing upright in the stone is a SWORD driven through an anvil set on the stone. T2: on the stone are letters written in gold that read 'WHOSO PULLETH OUT THIS SWORD OF THIS STONE AND ANVIL IS RIGHTWISE KING BORN OF ALL ENGLAND' (Malory Book I ch.5, near-verbatim from Caxton's text). Every knight and baron in the land tries and fails; the sword will not move. T3: at a tournament on New Year's day, a young squire named ARTHUR -- believed to be the son of SIR ECTOR and the foster-brother of Ector's son SIR KAY -- is sent back to fetch Kay's forgotten sword. Finding the inn locked, he rides to the churchyard, sees the sword in the stone, and DRAWS IT EASILY without knowing what it is. T4: when Ector sees the sword he takes Arthur back to the stone and makes him replace it and draw it again; then he and Kay kneel to Arthur. On CANDLEMAS, EASTER and PENTECOST the barons come and one after another still fail to draw the sword; only Arthur can pull it out, again and again, before the people; and at Pentecost the commons cry that they will have Arthur for their king. T5: Malory names this sword the SWORD OF THE STONE, and it is IMPORTANT that it is NOT Excalibur -- Arthur's stone-sword breaks in a later battle against KING PELLINORE, and Merlin then leads him to a lake where the LADY OF THE LAKE gives him the second, greater sword called Excalibur (Book I ch.25). Popular retellings collapse the two, but Malory's Arthur has TWO swords in Book I. Further rungs: the sword-in-the-stone motif is Robert de Boron's invention (Merlin, c.1200), not in Geoffrey of Monmouth; the earlier Geoffrey (Historia Regum Britanniae, c.1136) makes Arthur simply Uther's son crowned at fifteen with no sword-test; the Latin epithet 'rex quondam rexque futurus' ('the once and future king') will be inscribed on his tomb at the end of Malory Book XXI.
source: PRIMARY: Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book I chapters 5-7 (the sword and anvil in the London churchyard at Christmas; the gold-letter inscription 'Whoso pulleth out this sword'; Arthur as squire to Kay drawing it easily; the repeat draws at Candlemas, Easter, Pentecost; the commons acclaiming Arthur king) and Book I chapter 25 (the sword breaking against Pellinore and Merlin leading Arthur to the Lady of the Lake for Excalibur -- confirming these are TWO swords). Robert de Boron, Merlin (Old French verse c.1200 and later prose Estoire de Merlin) as the origin of the sword-in-stone motif. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Sword in the stone' and 'Excalibur' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Sword in the Stone', 'Excalibur', 'Robert de Boron', 'Le Morte d'Arthur' -- Malory Book I chapter numbering (Caxton edition), the inscription's wording, Arthur's foster-brother Kay, Sir Ector, the Pentecost crowning, the distinction between the stone-sword and Excalibur. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: verify the exact 'Whoso pulleth out' wording in the Caxton 1485 text (some modernisations render it 'whosoever' -- Malory's original is 'whoso').
framing_note: THE FOUNDATIONAL Arthurian ladder -- every kid knows the sword-in-the-stone image; the DINNER-TEST kicker is T5 (this is NOT Excalibur; there are TWO swords in Malory). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem describe a boy drawing a sword from a stone AND ask what happened -- describe the SCENE (Christmas in a London churchyard, gold letters on stone, a squire sent for his brother's sword) and let the recall be the BOY, the INSCRIPTION, or the BROTHER (Kay). Do not say 'Excalibur' anywhere in the stem or choices when asking about the stone-sword. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the Christian stories of prophecy-fulfilling children or the Norse stories of Sigurd's inheritance -- a hidden heir revealed by a test only he can pass. Do NOT use 'fulfilled the prophecy' framing; use 'the letters said, and only Arthur could do it'. DISTRACTOR MINE: other kings-by-token (Sigurd reforging Gram in the Volsung cycle; David chosen over his brothers by Samuel -- Christian pillar; Theseus lifting the rock for Aegeus's sword and sandals -- Greek pillar), other Malory swords (Excalibur, Balin's sword, Galahad's sword drawn from the floating stone at Camelot -- ADJACENT-real, especially the Galahad stone-sword which is a DIFFERENT scene in Book XIII). Wrong locations: the stone stands in a CHURCHYARD in LONDON, not at Camelot. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: Arthur may or may not have had a 6th-century British warlord original, but the sword-in-the-stone episode is PURE LEGEND -- Robert de Boron's c.1200 invention, not history. State this honestly if asked.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the actual sub-Roman British defence against the Saxons (c.500 AD, Battle of Badon) that some scholars think MIGHT have a historical Arthur-figure. Theology owns the STORY of the sword in the stone at London (pure Robert de Boron/Malory legend). No geography overlap -- the London churchyard is unspecified in Malory.

name: Uther Pendragon and Igraine: conception at Tintagel
scope: The magical begetting of Arthur, from Malory Book I chapters 1-3 (and going back to Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae Book VIII ch.19, c.1136). T1: UTHER PENDRAGON, King of Britain, falls violently in love with IGRAINE, the beautiful wife of GORLOIS, Duke of Cornwall. When Uther presses his suit at court Gorlois takes Igraine away and shuts her up in his fortress of TINTAGEL on the Cornish coast for safety. T2: Uther, sick with love, begs MERLIN the mage for help. Merlin agrees on ONE CONDITION -- that the child conceived that night shall be given to Merlin to raise as he sees fit. Uther swears it on the four Evangelists. T3: Merlin gives Uther a potion or charm that changes his SHAPE into the exact likeness of Duke GORLOIS -- beard, voice, armour, and all -- and changes two companions (Sir Ulfius and Sir Brastias in Malory; Ulfin in Geoffrey) into the shapes of Gorlois's chief knights. In this disguise Uther rides into Tintagel and is welcomed by Igraine as her husband. T4: THAT SAME NIGHT the real Gorlois is killed in a sortie outside his other castle at Dimilioc; and in Igraine's chamber at Tintagel, Uther in Gorlois's shape lies with her and conceives ARTHUR. When word comes at dawn that Gorlois is dead, Igraine realises the man in her bed cannot have been her husband and is silent, wondering. T5: Merlin comes for the child as promised; Arthur is given to SIR ECTOR and his wife to be raised in secret as their own son, not knowing he is a king's child. Uther marries Igraine soon after (making Arthur legitimate by later marriage in Malory's account) but Uther dies within two years and the land falls into anarchy until the sword in the stone appears. Further rungs: Geoffrey's 1136 Historia Regum Britanniae is the SOURCE of the Tintagel-shapechange story; Wace's Roman de Brut (c.1155) and Layamon's Brut (c.1215) transmit it into English; TINTAGEL as a place is a real 5th-6th century high-status Cornish site that WAS a stronghold in the sub-Roman period (archaeologists have found Mediterranean pottery there); the shape-change motif recurs in Celtic myth (see Cuchulainn's father Lugh visiting his mother in disguise).
source: PRIMARY: Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book I chapters 1-3 (Uther's love for Igraine; Gorlois taking her to Tintagel; Merlin's bargain and Uther's oath; the shape-change to Gorlois; the night at Tintagel; Gorlois's death that same night; Igraine's silence; Arthur given to Ector). ORIGINAL SOURCE: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII chapters 19-20 (c.1136 -- the shape-change episode invented). Wace, Roman de Brut (c.1155) and Layamon, Brut (c.1215) as the transmission line into English. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Uther Pendragon', 'Igraine', 'Tintagel' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Uther Pendragon', 'Igraine', 'Tintagel Castle', 'Historia Regum Britanniae' -- the shape-change, the oath about the child, Gorlois's simultaneous death, Arthur fostered by Ector. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether Malory attributes the shape-change to a POTION or a CHARM (Malory says Merlin 'changed the king's likeness' -- neutral).
framing_note: The ORIGIN ladder for the whole Arthurian cycle. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Merlin gives Uther the SHAPE of the man he is cuckolding) and T4 (Gorlois dies the SAME NIGHT, so Igraine's realisation comes at dawn). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Uther disguised as Gorlois' AND ask who he was disguised as -- describe the SCENE (a king in love, a rival's fortress on the Cornish coast, a mage's bargain, a shape-change spell) and let the recall be the DISGUISE, the PLACE (Tintagel), the MAGE, or the DUKE. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Zeus visiting Alcmene in the shape of Amphitryon (Greek pillar, the conception of Hercules -- literally the same shape-change motif) or the Christian Annunciation to Mary -- a legendary conception with a shape-change or visitation. Do NOT smirk at the ethics; state what Malory states, no editorial. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Merlin-shapechanges (there aren't many in Malory), other legendary conceptions (Hercules by Zeus-as-Amphitryon -- Greek; Cuchulainn by Lugh visiting Deichtine -- Irish pillar; Jesus by angel and Spirit -- Christian pillar), other Arthurian fathers (King Ban of Benwick who fathered Lancelot; King Pellinore who fathered Percival in Malory -- adjacent-real). Wrong castle: TINTAGEL, not Camelot; Camelot doesn't exist yet in this story. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: Tintagel is a REAL place with a real 5th-6th c. history; the shape-change story is pure 12th-century invention (Geoffrey of Monmouth).
history_overlap: HISTORY owns sub-Roman Britain and Tintagel as an archaeological site (Mediterranean pottery, 5th-6th c. high-status settlement). Theology owns the STORY of Uther, Igraine, and the shape-change conception at Tintagel. GEOGRAPHY owns Tintagel as a Cornish place; theology owns what HAPPENED there in the legend.

name: Merlin the mage: the wizard who arranges kings
scope: The figure of Merlin as the Arthurian court-mage, from Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae (c.1136), Robert de Boron's Merlin (c.1200), and Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur Books I-IV. T1: MERLIN (Latin Merlinus, from the Welsh Myrddin) is the MAGE and PROPHET at the centre of the young Arthur's court; he is the one who arranged Arthur's conception at Tintagel, took the child from Uther, gave him to Sir Ector to raise, and made the sword-in-the-stone test that would prove him king. T2: in Robert de Boron's Merlin (c.1200), Merlin is the son of a DEMON father and a virtuous mortal mother -- the demons meant to create an antichrist to counter Christ's birth, but the mother's confession and baptism turned the child's gifts to good; Merlin has the demons' knowledge of the past AND (from God) knowledge of the future. T3: Merlin's most famous single act (from Geoffrey's Historia Regum Britanniae Book VIII) is bringing STONEHENGE from Ireland: the giants had built it there long ago, and Merlin uses his magic to LIFT the stones over the Irish Sea and set them on Salisbury Plain as a memorial to the British nobles massacred by Hengist. T4: in Malory Merlin also RAISES the ROUND TABLE (from King Uther, who had it from Leodegrance's father), gives Arthur the geography of his own future battles, and warns him at every step -- but his greatest quality is that he FORETELLS EVERY DISASTER OF ARTHUR'S REIGN, INCLUDING HIS OWN, and cannot prevent any of them because knowing the future does not confer power to change it. T5: Merlin's own downfall comes when he falls in love with a lady of the Lake called NIMUE (or Viviane in the French tradition); she coaxes his spells out of him one by one, then uses one of them to seal him forever inside a ROCK (Malory Book IV ch.1) or inside a HAWTHORN TREE (Post-Vulgate) or a cave in the forest of Broceliande (French romance). He does not die -- he sleeps, and can be heard calling out under the stone. Further rungs: the historical figure of Myrddin Wyllt in Welsh tradition (a 6th-century mad prophet in the woods, distinct from Merlin the wizard); Geoffrey of Monmouth's separate Vita Merlini (c.1150) has the mad-prophet version; the fusion into Malory's court-mage is Geoffrey's synthesis; Merlin as an ARCHETYPE (the wise old wizard) is the source of Gandalf, Dumbledore, and every wizard-mentor in modern fantasy.
source: PRIMARY: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae Book VI ch.19 (Merlin prophesying), Book VIII ch.10-12 (Merlin moving the giants' dance to Salisbury Plain -- Stonehenge), Book VIII ch.19-20 (the Tintagel shape-change). Robert de Boron, Merlin (c.1200 -- Merlin's demon-parentage). Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Books I-IV (Merlin at Arthur's court; the giving of Excalibur; the warnings Arthur ignores; Book IV ch.1 for Merlin's sealing by Nimue). Geoffrey of Monmouth, Vita Merlini (c.1150 -- the mad-prophet version). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Merlin' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Merlin', 'Myrddin Wyllt', 'Robert de Boron', 'Vita Merlini' -- Merlin's demon-father parentage, Stonehenge origin story, court-mage role, Nimue and the rock, the Broceliande version. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether Malory names the entrapping stone as a 'stone', 'cave', or 'cavern' (Malory Book IV ch.1 has 'a great stone').
framing_note: The MENTOR-ARCHETYPE ladder -- Merlin sits behind Arthur's whole life. Dinner-test payoffs: T2 (his FATHER was a DEMON; the antichrist plot went wrong) and T3 (he MOVED STONEHENGE from Ireland by magic). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the wizard of Arthur's court' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (an old mage arranging the sword-test, a boy taken from a Cornish castle, prophecies Arthur refuses to heed) and let the recall be the WIZARD, his ORIGIN, or his TRAP. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Chiron the centaur teaching Achilles (Greek pillar), Odin as All-Father teaching Sigurd (Norse pillar), or Elijah training Elisha (Christian pillar) -- an old wise figure shaping a hero. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Arthurian magic-workers (Morgan le Fay, Nimue herself, the Lady of the Lake, Ninianne), other legendary wizards (Gandalf and Dumbledore are DERIVATIVE, don't use), the two Merlins (Myrddin Wyllt the mad prophet vs Merlin Ambrosius the court-mage -- Geoffrey's own fusion). Wrong parent: Merlin's father is a DEMON (in de Boron), not a god or a king. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: Merlin as court-mage is 12th-century legend; the Welsh Myrddin Wyllt as historical mad-prophet is 6th-century tradition. State honestly.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Stonehenge as a real Neolithic monument; theology owns the LEGEND that Merlin moved it from Ireland (Geoffrey of Monmouth). HISTORY owns the Welsh Myrddin traditions as post-Roman British material.

name: Excalibur and the Lady of the Lake
scope: Arthur's second, greater sword from Malory Book I chapter 25 (Caxton 1485). T1: after Arthur breaks his first sword (the one drawn from the stone) in single combat with KING PELLINORE, MERLIN takes him riding through the country until they come to a wide LAKE with a low island in the middle. T2: in the middle of the lake Arthur sees a WOMAN'S ARM CLOTHED IN WHITE SAMITE (a rich silk) rise up out of the water, and in the hand is a SWORD held aloft above the surface. T3: Merlin tells Arthur that this sword is called EXCALIBUR -- 'that is as much to say as CUT-STEEL' (Malory Book I ch.25) -- and that a lady called the LADY OF THE LAKE has given it to him. Arthur is to row out in a barge, take the sword and the scabbard, and thank her. Arthur does so; the arm sinks back beneath the water. T4: Merlin then asks Arthur which he likes better, the sword or the scabbard. Arthur says the SWORD. Merlin rebukes him: 'YE ARE THE MORE UNWISE, for the SCABBARD IS WORTH TEN OF THE SWORD -- for whiles ye have the scabbard upon you, ye shall never lose no blood, be ye never so sore wounded' (Malory Book I ch.25, near-verbatim). Excalibur's scabbard makes its bearer INVULNERABLE. T5: this scabbard is later STOLEN by Arthur's half-sister MORGAN LE FAY and thrown into a deep lake so he can never find it; without it Arthur can bleed and die, and he will (Malory Book IV ch.14). At the last battle at CAMLANN the mortally wounded Arthur orders SIR BEDIVERE to throw Excalibur itself back into a lake -- and on the third throw the arm rises and catches it (its own ladder). Further rungs: Excalibur is the OLD FRENCH form 'Escalibor' from Latin 'Caliburnus' from Welsh 'Caledfwlch' ('hard-cleaver') in the earliest Welsh Arthurian tale Culhwch and Olwen (c.1100); Geoffrey of Monmouth already has Caliburnus as Arthur's sword (Historia Regum Britanniae Book IX ch.4); the sword-from-the-lake tradition is distinct from the sword-in-the-stone tradition and popular retellings COLLAPSE the two.
source: PRIMARY: Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book I chapter 25 (Arthur's stone-sword broken against Pellinore; Merlin taking him to the lake; the arm in white samite; the sword Excalibur -- 'cut-steel'; the scabbard worth ten of the sword; Arthur's promise never to lose blood while wearing it) and Book IV chapter 14 (Morgan le Fay stealing the scabbard). ORIGINAL: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae Book IX ch.4 (Caliburnus, forged in Avalon). Welsh: Culhwch and Olwen (c.1100 -- Caledfwlch, the Welsh name behind Excalibur). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Excalibur' and 'Lady of the Lake' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Excalibur', 'Lady of the Lake', 'Caliburnus', 'Caledfwlch' -- the two-swords distinction, the white samite arm, Malory's 'worth ten of the sword' passage, Morgan's theft of the scabbard, the Welsh Caledfwlch origin. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: verify the Malory Book I ch.25 exact wording of 'ten of the sword' (some editions render 'worth ten of the swords').
framing_note: THE signature-artifact ladder of the pillar -- Excalibur is Arthurian myth's most famous object. Dinner-test payoffs: T4 (the SCABBARD is worth TEN OF THE SWORD, and its owner CANNOT BLEED) and T3 (Excalibur means 'CUT-STEEL' in Malory's gloss). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem describe a magic sword given by a lake-arm AND ask its name; describe the SCENE (a barge on a wide lake, a woman's arm in white silk holding a blade above the water) and let the recall be the SWORD, the SCABBARD's power, the GIVER, or the ORIGINAL owner (the Lady of the Lake). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Sigurd's sword Gram reforged from the pieces (Norse pillar), Achilles's shield made by Hephaestus (Greek pillar), or Roland's Durendal (Western-medieval pillar) -- a hero's signature weapon with a named origin and a named property. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Arthurian swords (the sword drawn from the stone -- THE OTHER Arthur sword, must be distinguished; Galahad's sword drawn from the floating stone at Camelot; Balin's fatal sword; Gawain's Galatine; Lancelot's sword), other magic-invulnerability items (the Ring of Gyges -- Greek philosophy; the Belt of Achilles's mother; Sigurd's dragon-blood bath making him invulnerable-except-shoulder -- Norse). WRONG GIVER: the Lady of the Lake gives Excalibur; Merlin BROKERS the gift but does not make the sword. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: EXCALIBUR IS PURE LEGEND -- state this if asked. The name has Welsh roots (Caledfwlch); the story is myth.
history_overlap: None with history -- Excalibur is pure legend. No geography overlap -- the lake is unnamed in Malory.

name: Camelot and the Round Table
scope: Arthur's capital and its famous piece of furniture, from Chretien de Troyes (first named 'Camelot' in Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart, c.1177) and Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur Book III chapter 1. T1: CAMELOT is the CAPITAL city of King Arthur's Britain, the seat of his court, the hall where his knights feast, and the destination of every quest that ends well. T2: at Camelot stands the great ROUND TABLE -- a table with NO HEAD and no foot, so that every knight seated at it is EQUAL in dignity, none set above another. T3: the Round Table is not Arthur's original property. Malory tells (Book III ch.1) that it came to him as a WEDDING GIFT from GUINEVERE'S FATHER, KING LEODEGRANCE of Cameliard, when Arthur married Guinevere. Leodegrance had it from Uther Pendragon, who had it from Merlin, who had it made in the first place. It seats 150 knights (Malory), and every seat has the name of the knight who is worthy to sit there written in gold. T4: one seat -- called the SIEGE PERILOUS (the 'perilous seat', 'Sege Perelous' in Malory) -- is left empty because ANY KNIGHT WHO SITS IN IT WHO IS NOT PERFECTLY PURE will DIE ON THE SPOT. Only ONE knight in all the story is worthy to sit in it and live: GALAHAD, son of Lancelot, who arrives at Pentecost and sits down as the letters on the seat appear (Malory Book XIII ch.4). T5: the shape of the table -- circular, no head, all equal -- is the STORY MEANING of Arthurian kingship: not a tyrant on a throne with vassals below him, but a company of equals held together by the code of chivalry, of whom the king is only the FIRST. When the fellowship of the Round Table breaks (Book XX-XXI), the whole civilisation goes with it. Further rungs: Chretien de Troyes NAMES 'Camelot' in one line of Lancelot le Chevalier de la Charrette (c.1177) -- just 'in a town called Camelot' -- and it becomes the standard name afterwards; the Round Table motif is INVENTED by Wace, Roman de Brut (c.1155), as Arthur's fix for the rank-quarrels that plagued Uther's court; the SIEGE PERILOUS is developed most fully in the Vulgate Cycle Queste del Saint Graal (c.1220) and passed to Malory; the real medieval 'Winchester Round Table' hanging in Winchester Castle's Great Hall is a 13th-14th century oak roundel painted for a Tudor king (Henry VIII) -- REAL object, not the real Round Table.
source: PRIMARY: Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book III chapter 1 (Leodegrance's wedding-gift of the Round Table, seating 150), Book XIII chapter 4 (Galahad's arrival, the Siege Perilous). Chretien de Troyes, Lancelot, le Chevalier de la Charrette (c.1177 -- first appearance of the name Camelot). Wace, Roman de Brut (c.1155 -- invention of the Round Table). Vulgate Cycle, La Queste del Saint Graal (c.1220 -- development of the Siege Perilous). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Camelot' and 'Round Table' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Camelot', 'Round Table', 'Siege Perilous', 'Winchester Round Table' -- Chretien's naming, Leodegrance's gift, Malory's 150 seats, Galahad and the Siege Perilous, the Winchester Round Table object. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: Malory's exact seat-count for the Round Table (150 in some editions, 140 or 'more than a hundred' in others).
framing_note: The PLACE + FURNITURE ladder -- Camelot and its table are the setting of every downstream story. Dinner-test payoffs: T3 (the table was a WEDDING GIFT from Guinevere's father, not Arthur's own creation) and T4 (there is a seat that KILLS anyone unworthy who sits in it). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the seat that killed the unworthy' AND ask its name; describe the SCENE (a round table in Camelot, 150 knights seating equal, one seat always empty at the table's edge) and let the recall be the SEAT, the KNIGHT who filled it, or the WEDDING GIFTER (Leodegrance). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Odin's hall Valhalla with its 540 doors (Norse pillar), Olympus with the twelve thrones (Greek pillar), or Solomon's temple with the two pillars Jachin and Boaz (Christian pillar) -- the great hall/table of a mythic order. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Arthurian objects (Excalibur, the Grail, the sword-in-the-stone), other famous tables/thrones (Odin's high seat Hlidskjalf, Solomon's throne, the Iron Throne -- silly-modern, don't use), other knights linked to the Siege Perilous (Percival the Grail-knight sits at a DIFFERENT seat; Lancelot never sits there -- only Galahad). Wrong gifter: LEODEGRANCE (Guinevere's father), not Arthur, not Merlin. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: 'Camelot' as a place is Chretien's invention (c.1177); Cadbury Castle and Winchester have both been proposed as 'the real Camelot' but neither is proven.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Winchester and Cadbury as real sites (some 6th-c. reoccupation at Cadbury) and the Winchester Round Table object as a genuine 13th-14th c. artifact. Theology owns the STORY of Camelot and the wedding-gift Round Table (pure legend). No geography overlap unless a specific site is mentioned.

name: Guinevere: the queen at the stake
scope: Queen Guinevere, her love affair with Lancelot, and the burning that Lancelot prevents, from Malory Le Morte d'Arthur Book XX chapters 1-8. T1: GUINEVERE (Old French Guenievre, from Welsh Gwenhwyfar meaning 'white phantom') is the QUEEN of Arthur -- daughter of King Leodegrance of Cameliard, whom Arthur marries as a young king (against Merlin's warnings), receiving the Round Table itself as her dowry. T2: Guinevere and SIR LANCELOT of the Lake, the greatest of Arthur's knights, are lovers in secret for many years. The love affair is central to Chretien de Troyes's Lancelot, le Chevalier de la Charrette (c.1177) -- where Chretien invents Lancelot as a knight so devoted to the queen that he rides in a cart of shame to rescue her -- and it runs through the whole of Malory's Books XVIII-XX. T3: Sir AGRAVAINE (Gawain's brother) and Sir MORDRED expose the lovers: they trap Lancelot in the queen's chamber with twelve armed knights outside the door. Lancelot fights his way out, killing thirteen knights including Agravaine. Guinevere is arrested, and Arthur -- required by his own law -- CONDEMNS HIS QUEEN TO BE BURNED AT THE STAKE for treason (Malory Book XX ch.7). T4: at the pyre in the courtyard at Carlisle, dressed in her SMOCK, Guinevere is led out to be burned. LANCELOT and his kin ride in at full charge, cut through the guard, sweep the queen up ONTO HIS HORSE, and ride away. But in the melee Lancelot's sword kills SIR GARETH (Beaumains) and SIR GAHERIS, unarmed brothers of Gawain -- and Gawain, who had loved Lancelot best, from that hour becomes his mortal enemy and pushes Arthur to war against him. T5: this rescue is the moment the FELLOWSHIP OF THE ROUND TABLE BREAKS -- Lancelot and his kin flee to France; Arthur besieges Lancelot's castle; Mordred (left as regent) seizes the throne; Camlann follows. Guinevere, when Arthur is dead, becomes a NUN at AMESBURY and dies there in penance, refusing to see Lancelot when he comes for her one last time (Malory Book XXI ch.7-11). Further rungs: the earliest Guinevere-Lancelot story is Chretien's Charrette (c.1177) -- the 'cart' of the title is a cart of shame Lancelot rides in to reach the queen; the SMOCK detail at the pyre is Malory's; Guinevere as an ADULTERESS-QUEEN whose sin ends a kingdom parallels Helen of Troy (Greek pillar) and Isolde with Tristan (Arthurian pillar).

Chretien de Troyes, Lancelot, le Chevalier de la Charrette (c.1177 -- the invention of Lancelot as Guinevere's lover and the cart-of-shame). name: Lancelot of the Lake: the greatest knight and his madness
scope: Lancelot's origin, his supremacy in arms, and his madness in the wilderness, from Chretien de Troyes's Lancelot (c.1177), the Vulgate Cycle Lancelot en prose (c.1215-30), and Malory Books VI, XI-XII. T1: SIR LANCELOT is called LANCELOT OF THE LAKE -- 'du Lac' in French -- because as an infant he was taken from his father KING BAN of Benwick (who died in war against King Claudas of Gaul) by the LADY OF THE LAKE, VIVIANE, and raised UNDERWATER in her enchanted lake-kingdom until he was old enough to be sent to Arthur's court. He does not know his own name for years; the Lady names him. T2: Lancelot is the GREATEST KNIGHT of the Round Table -- undefeated in single combat, first in every tournament, the one Arthur trusts most. Chretien's Lancelot le Chevalier de la Charrette (c.1177) is the ORIGIN romance for this figure: Chretien writes him as the queen's lover who rides in a cart of shame (a criminal's cart) to rescue Guinevere from Meleagant. T3: Lancelot is also GUINEVERE'S SECRET LOVER, and the tension between his love for the queen and his knightly duty to Arthur runs the whole cycle. When Elaine of Corbenic tricks him one night into thinking she is Guinevere and conceives GALAHAD, and Guinevere later discovers Elaine at court, Guinevere's fury drives Lancelot INSANE and he runs mad into the woods for TWO YEARS, forgotten by all, eating with hermits and shepherds. T4: eventually the wandering mad Lancelot is brought to CORBENIC, the GRAIL CASTLE ruled by King Pelles (Elaine's father). The keepers set him to sleep in a chamber where a covered Grail passes by in the night, and he is HEALED by its power (Malory Book XII ch.4). Restored, he returns to Camelot but never fully to his old strength -- because Grail-mystery has laid its hand on him and he is not pure enough to see it fully. T5: Lancelot's FINAL story is grief. He rescues Guinevere from the pyre (see her ladder), accidentally kills Gareth, causes the war that breaks Camelot, loses Guinevere to the nunnery at Amesbury, and ends his own life as a HERMIT at Glastonbury with a few companions; when he dies (Malory Book XXI ch.13) they see his body lying with a smile on his face, and the bishop dreams of angels lifting Lancelot up to heaven despite his sins. Further rungs: Chretien's Charrette is the earliest surviving Lancelot romance and INVENTS him as Guinevere's lover; the Vulgate Cycle (c.1215-30) is where the underwater-fostering by the Lady of the Lake is developed; the madness-in-the-woods motif is a widespread Celtic pattern (Suibhne Geilt in Irish; Myrddin Wyllt in Welsh); Lancelot's son Galahad is the PURE knight Lancelot could not be.

name: Galahad: the perfect knight and the Siege Perilous
scope: The pure Grail-knight, from the Vulgate Queste del Saint Graal (c.1220) and Malory Le Morte d'Arthur Books XIII-XVII (Caxton 1485). T1: SIR GALAHAD is the son of SIR LANCELOT and ELAINE of Corbenic (daughter of King Pelles the Fisher King -- see the Grail Castle ladders). Elaine tricked Lancelot into sleeping with her one night by enchantment (he thought she was Guinevere); the child conceived is Galahad. Galahad is raised in a nunnery, unknown to Lancelot, and comes to Camelot as a young knight of about fifteen. T2: at PENTECOST, an unknown young knight in RED ARMOUR is brought into Camelot by an old hermit and led to the ROUND TABLE. The company sees that the letters on the SIEGE PERILOUS -- the empty perilous seat that KILLS any impure knight who sits in it -- now read 'THIS IS THE SIEGE OF GALAHAD, THE HAUT PRINCE'. Galahad sits down; nothing happens; he is the one for whom the seat was reserved (Malory Book XIII ch.4). T3: on the same day a FLOATING STONE with a SWORD in it comes up the river to Camelot; letters on the stone say only he who is the best knight in the world shall draw it. Lancelot and Gawain try and fail; Galahad puts his hand to it and DRAWS IT EASILY (Malory Book XIII ch.2) -- the second sword-in-a-stone of the cycle, this one Galahad's alone. T4: Galahad leads the Grail Quest. Only three knights of Arthur's fellowship achieve the Grail: GALAHAD, PERCIVAL and BORS. They come to the castle of CORBENIC and see the Grail uncovered in the chapel. Christ himself steps out of the Grail vessel and gives them communion. T5: Galahad asks that he may die at the moment of his greatest joy. In the city of SARRAS (a mystical city, sometimes placed in the East), Galahad becomes king for a year, and then during a Mass he beholds the Grail directly and the wonder KILLS HIM with joy -- his soul is carried up by angels, and a hand descends from heaven and takes the Grail away, and it is never seen again in this world (Malory Book XVII ch.22). Percival dies a hermit soon after; Bors alone returns to Camelot to tell the tale. Further rungs: Galahad is a LATE addition to the cycle -- the Vulgate Queste (c.1220, part of the Cistercian-influenced Vulgate Cycle) INVENTS him as the pure knight Lancelot cannot be; earlier romances (Chretien's Perceval) have PERCEVAL as the Grail-knight; the Siege Perilous is developed in the Queste; the FLOATING-STONE-WITH-SWORD is a deliberate echo of Arthur's boyhood sword-in-the-stone (a new king of holiness paralleling a new king of Britain).

Dinner-test payoffs: T2 (he is the ONLY knight who can sit in the DEATH-SEAT and live) and T5 (he asks to DIE at the moment of his greatest joy, and gets his wish). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the pure knight who achieved the Grail' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a fifteen-year-old in red armour at Pentecost, an empty seat with new gold letters, a floating stone with a sword drifting up the river, a chapel where Christ steps from a cup) and let the recall be the KNIGHT, the SEAT, the FATHER (Lancelot), or the CITY (Sarras). DISTRACTOR MINE: other Grail knights (Percival, Bors -- the OTHER TWO who achieve the Grail; Lancelot who is NOT pure enough), other pure-and-perfect figures (Baldr in Norse pillar; Galahad's father Lancelot who is his opposite), other seats-of-death (there is only ONE Siege Perilous). Wrong father: LANCELOT (not Percival, not Gawain). Wrong mother: ELAINE OF CORBENIC (King Pelles's daughter), not Elaine of Astolat (the tragic lily-maiden who loves Lancelot separately).

name: Perceval and the Fisher King: the question he failed to ask
scope: The country boy who becomes a Grail knight and the question he fatally fails to ask, from Chretien de Troyes's PERCEVAL, LE CONTE DU GRAAL (c.1181-90, unfinished at Chretien's death). T1: PERCEVAL (French Perceval; Welsh Peredur; German Parzival) is a country boy raised in the WELSH FOREST by his widowed mother, who has kept him ignorant of KNIGHTHOOD to protect him -- his father and brothers were all killed as knights. When Perceval one day sees five knights in armour riding through the forest, he thinks they are angels; he leaves home for Arthur's court against his mother's begging, and his mother DIES OF GRIEF at his departure. T2: after adventures at Camelot and knighthood at the hands of Gornemant, Perceval one evening is riding by a river and sees a MAN FISHING FROM A BOAT. The Fisherman invites him to his castle for the night; when Perceval arrives at the CASTLE (unnamed by Chretien; later called Corbenic), he finds the same man now seated in a hall on a couch, WOUNDED, unable to walk -- the FISHER KING. T3: as they sit at supper a wonderful PROCESSION passes through the hall: a young man carrying a SPEAR from whose tip a DROP OF BLOOD constantly falls; two young men with candelabra; a maiden carrying a bright GRAAL (a shallow dish or platter -- the word in Chretien's Old French is 'graal' and means simply 'a wide serving-dish'); a second maiden with a SILVER PLATTER. They pass through the hall from door to door. T4: Perceval, remembering Gornemant's teaching that a knight should NOT ASK IDLE QUESTIONS, holds his tongue -- and does NOT ASK 'WHOM DOES THE GRAIL SERVE?' or 'WHY DOES THE SPEAR BLEED?'. He goes to bed silent. In the morning the castle is EMPTY -- everyone gone. When he rides out, the drawbridge slams up behind him, and a maiden in the woods tells him: had he ASKED the question, the wounded Fisher King would have been HEALED and his land restored; his silence has doomed the Waste Land to remain waste. T5: Chretien's poem BREAKS OFF unfinished at this point (Chretien died c.1191), and the story of Perceval's return and healing of the Fisher King is completed only in later 'Continuations' by other hands and in Wolfram von Eschenbach's PARZIVAL (c.1210). The 'question' Perceval fails to ask -- COMPASSION over politeness, engagement over correctness -- is the mystical heart of the whole Grail cycle. Further rungs: Chretien's Perceval le Conte du Graal (c.1181-90) is the FIRST Grail romance in any language; the word 'graal' in Chretien means only a wide serving-dish, not yet a cup; the identification of the Grail with the Last Supper cup is Robert de Boron's addition (c.1200); the Welsh analogue is Peredur son of Efrawg (part of the Mabinogion) which lacks the Grail question and has a severed head on a platter instead; Wagner's opera Parsifal (1882) is Wolfram's version staged.

name: Gawain and the Green Knight: the beheading game
scope: The alliterative Middle English poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (Cotton Nero A.x, c.1400) -- a beheading bargain and a girdle. T1: on NEW YEAR'S DAY at Camelot, Arthur's court is at feast when a huge KNIGHT rides in on horseback -- and everything about him is GREEN. Green skin, green armour, green horse; in one hand a great AXE, in the other a bough of HOLLY. He challenges any man of the court to a Christmas GAME: 'STRIKE ME ONE BLOW with this axe, and a year and a day from now come and let me strike you one blow in return' (Fitt I). T2: the whole court is silent. Arthur himself starts to rise to take up the challenge, but SIR GAWAIN, Arthur's nephew and the youngest of his best knights, asks leave to take the game in his uncle's place. Gawain swings the axe and STRIKES OFF THE GREEN KNIGHT'S HEAD in a single blow. The head rolls on the floor. T3: the headless Green Knight PICKS UP HIS OWN HEAD by the hair, walks calmly to his horse, mounts, and holds the head up to face Gawain. The eyes open; the head SPEAKS, telling Gawain to meet him a year hence at the GREEN CHAPEL for his return-blow. The Green Knight rides out, hoofbeats fading, and the court is silent (end of Fitt I). T4: a year later Gawain rides north through winter and comes at Christmas to a castle in the wilds, kept by LORD BERTILAK and his LADY. Bertilak makes an inner bargain: while Bertilak hunts each day, Gawain will rest at the castle, and each night they will EXCHANGE what each has won. Bertilak's lady comes to Gawain's chamber and tries to seduce him each day; Gawain each night gives Bertilak the kisses she gave him. On the third day she also gives Gawain a GREEN GIRDLE (a silk belt) which she swears will keep its wearer from being wounded. Fearing his death tomorrow, Gawain KEEPS the girdle and does not give it to Bertilak -- breaking the game (Fitt III). T5: on New Year's Day Gawain rides to the GREEN CHAPEL and finds the Green Knight sharpening his axe by a stream. Gawain bares his neck. The first swing the Green Knight PULLS UP -- because Gawain FLINCHED. Second swing -- pulled up again, because Gawain kept his nerve. THIRD swing comes down and just NICKS Gawain's neck, drawing a drop of BLOOD (Fitt IV). The Green Knight reveals himself -- he is LORD BERTILAK, transformed by the enchantress MORGAN LE FAY (whom Gawain met at the castle without knowing her); the nick was for the one day Gawain hid the girdle. Gawain rides back to Camelot in shame with the green girdle around his shoulder like a badge -- and the whole court decides to wear a green sash in his honour (Fitt IV, closing lines). Further rungs: the poem survives in a SINGLE manuscript, British Library Cotton Nero A.x, c.1400, in a Northwest Midlands dialect, by an unknown poet (called simply 'the Gawain-poet' or 'the Pearl-poet' because the same manuscript contains three other poems -- Pearl, Cleanness, Patience -- believed to be by the same hand); the Green Knight's colour + holly bough echo the medieval Green Man carving found in English parish churches; the beheading game is a common Celtic motif (Bricriu's Feast in the Irish Ulster Cycle has an almost identical scene with Cuchulainn accepting the game).

ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the knight who plays the beheading game' AND ask which one; describe the SCENE (a green knight on a green horse at Camelot on New Year's, a holly bough and an axe, a picked-up head that speaks) and let the recall be the KNIGHT (Gawain), the GAME-MASTER (the Green Knight / Bertilak), the OBJECT (green girdle), or the FORCE BEHIND IT (Morgan le Fay). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the beheading game in Bricriu's Feast (Celtic pillar -- direct source-analogue), or Odysseus and the Cyclops's cave (Greek pillar) -- a mortal caught in a monster's game with rules he must survive. Emphasise the poem's ARTISTRY -- alliterative Middle English, single manuscript, the four Fitts, Cotton Nero A.x. DISTRACTOR MINE: other beheading games (Cuchulainn in Bricriu's Feast -- Celtic-Irish pillar, the direct analogue), other three-swings-with-an-axe scenes (there isn't a well-known one), other green-clad figures (the Green Man of church carvings; Robin Hood in Lincoln green -- Robin is unrelated), other Arthurian tests (the Siege Perilous, the sword in the stone). Wrong sender: MORGAN LE FAY sends the Green Knight to test Camelot, not Merlin, not Nimue. Wrong location: the GREEN CHAPEL (a mound/cave in the north wilderness), not any specific real chapel.

name: Mordred and the Battle of Camlann
scope: Arthur's incestuous son, the treacherous regent, and the last battle, from Malory Book XXI (Caxton 1485) and going back through the Vulgate Mort Artu (c.1230) to Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae Book XI (c.1136) and the earlier Welsh annals. T1: MORDRED is Arthur's SON, born of INCEST. In Malory (Book I ch.19-20), the young Arthur unknowingly sleeps with MORGAUSE, wife of King Lot of Orkney -- who is Arthur's HALF-SISTER (both children of Igraine, Morgause by her first husband Gorlois of Cornwall). Merlin later reveals the relationship and prophesies that the child of this union will DESTROY THE KINGDOM. In the older French tradition Mordred is Arthur's son by MORGAN LE FAY (also his half-sister); Malory's choice of Morgause is idiosyncratic. T2: Arthur, when told of the prophecy, has all the noble children born in May sent out to sea in a boat to be lost -- the boat wrecks but Mordred survives, is raised in secret, and grows up to come to court as a young knight, half-brother to Gawain and eventually one of the fellowship of the Round Table. T3: while Arthur is across the Channel besieging Lancelot at Benwick after the affair with Guinevere is exposed, MORDRED IS LEFT AS REGENT of Britain. Mordred forges a letter saying Arthur is dead, has himself CROWNED KING, and tries to force Guinevere to marry him. Guinevere shuts herself up in the TOWER OF LONDON to escape him (Malory Book XXI ch.1). T4: Arthur races home from France with his army. Mordred meets him with an army of Saxons and rebels on the plain of CAMLANN in the west of Britain (Cornwall or Somerset in most traditions; the Welsh annals give the year 537). Peace-talks are agreed for the morning of the battle; the two armies drawn up facing each other under a truce -- one knight is stung by an ADDER in the heather, DRAWS HIS SWORD to kill it, and the drawn sword is taken as a signal of treachery; both armies charge. T5: the battle at Camlann lasts all day; by evening every knight of the Round Table on both sides is DEAD except Arthur, Sir Bedivere, and Sir Lucan. Arthur sees MORDRED alone across the field, leaning on his sword among the dead. Arthur takes his spear and drives it through Mordred's body clean; Mordred, dying, PULLS HIMSELF UP the shaft of the spear until he can reach Arthur, and gives him a mortal wound in the head with his sword (Malory Book XXI ch.4). Both fall. Arthur, mortally wounded, is carried from the field. Further rungs: the earliest surviving reference to Camlann is in the Welsh Annals (Annales Cambriae) under the year 537: 'the strife of Camlann in which Arthur and Medraut fell' -- Medraut is the Welsh name for Mordred, and this bare line is the OLDEST Arthurian reference outside the pure legend; Geoffrey of Monmouth (Historia Regum Britanniae XI, c.1136) is the first to make Mordred a treacherous regent; the incest with Morgause is Vulgate/Malory; the ADDER-IN-THE-HEATHER scene is Malory's; the Camlann pattern (a great order's LAST battle where friend and foe die together) parallels Ragnarok (Norse pillar) and the Song of Roland at Roncesvalles (Western-medieval pillar).
source: PRIMARY: Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book I chapters 19-20 (Arthur's night with Morgause; Merlin's prophecy), Book XXI chapters 1-4 (Mordred's regency, forged letter, seizure of the crown, Guinevere in the Tower, Camlann, the adder-in-the-heather, the death of Mordred and mortal wounding of Arthur). Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book XI (c.1136 -- Mordred as treacherous regent, the last battle). Vulgate Cycle, La Mort le roi Artu (c.1230). Welsh: Annales Cambriae s.a. 537 -- 'the strife of Camlann in which Arthur and Medraut fell' (earliest reference outside pure legend). Wrong mother: MALORY says MORGAUSE (Arthur's half-sister via Igraine and Gorlois); the FRENCH tradition says MORGAN LE FAY (also half-sister). Name the version. name: Bedivere and the returning of Excalibur
scope: The last scene between Arthur and his sword, from Malory Book XXI chapter 5 (Caxton 1485), going back to Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae Book XI. T1: after the Battle of CAMLANN, the mortally wounded ARTHUR is carried off the field with only two knights still alive -- his cupbearer SIR LUCAN, who dies of his wounds while lifting the king, and SIR BEDIVERE the one-handed, oldest of his companions. T2: Arthur, weakening fast, orders BEDIVERE to take EXCALIBUR and go to the nearby WATER (a lake or a mere in Malory; Geoffrey has a river) and THROW THE SWORD FAR OUT INTO THE WATER, then come back and tell what he sees. T3: Bedivere goes to the water; but when he sees Excalibur's pommel of precious stones and gold he thinks it a WASTE to lose it, and HIDES IT under a tree. He comes back and says he saw only 'the WIND on the water and the waves'. Arthur, knowing he lies, sends him back a SECOND TIME. Bedivere goes, looks at the sword again, HIDES IT AGAIN, and returns saying only he saw 'the waters wan and the waves wap'. Arthur rebukes him: 'YE THAT HAVE BEEN TO ME SO LIEF AND DEAR -- and thou shouldst betray me for the riches of a sword?' (Malory Book XXI ch.5, near-verbatim). T4: on the THIRD TIME Bedivere at last takes the sword by the girdle, WHIRLS it, and throws it AS FAR OUT INTO THE WATER as his strength will send it. Then -- and only then -- an ARM RISES UP from the water 'CLOTHED IN WHITE SAMITE', CATCHES the sword three times, brandishes it, and sinks with it beneath the surface (Malory Book XXI ch.5). Bedivere returns and tells Arthur what he saw; and now Arthur believes he has been obeyed. T5: this scene closes the Excalibur story that opened in Book I ch.25 -- an arm in white samite gave the sword UP to Arthur out of a lake, and now an arm in white samite takes it BACK. Arthur is then carried to the water's edge and put into a barge with three queens weeping over him (see next ladder). Further rungs: the three-tries pattern (twice failed, third time succeeded) is a fundamental Arthurian and Celtic storytelling shape; Malory's phrase 'the waters wan and the waves wap' is one of the most quoted single lines in the whole Morte d'Arthur; the arm from the lake mirrors Book I exactly -- the swordbelt (girdle) round Excalibur that Bedivere winds up to throw is a small detail from Malory; the returning of the great sword closes the circle of the whole legend.
source: PRIMARY: Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI chapter 5 (mortally wounded Arthur; Bedivere's two lies about waves and wind; Arthur's rebuke; the third throw; the arm in white samite catching the sword). Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book XI (older bare version -- Arthur's wounding and Avalon, sword not present). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Sir Bedivere' and 'Excalibur' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Bedivere', 'Excalibur', 'Le Morte d'Arthur' -- Bedivere as one of the two survivors, the three attempts, the exact wording of Malory's 'waters wan and the waves wap', the arm in white samite, the girdle-wind-throw. Tennyson, Idylls of the King, 'The Passing of Arthur' (Victorian retelling of the same scene, with 'Sir Bedivere the last of all his knights'). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact wording of Malory's Book XXI ch.5 in the Caxton text vs the Winchester manuscript.
framing_note: The CLOSING-SCENE ladder -- pure story-craft, three tries and a returning symmetry with the opening. Dinner-test payoffs: T3 (Bedivere LIES TWICE about what he saw at the water) and T4 (the third time an arm CATCHES the sword and brandishes it before sinking). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the knight who threw Excalibur back into the water' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a dying king by a lake, an old one-handed knight ordered to throw a jewelled sword away, two lies, a third throw) and let the recall be the KNIGHT (Bedivere), the SWORD, the NUMBER of tries (three), or WHAT the arm did (caught, brandished, sank). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Odysseus's arrow through the axe-handles at the return to Ithaca (Greek pillar), or the Norse ravens Huginn and Muninn flying home to Odin (Norse pillar) -- an image that closes a hero's story. DISTRACTOR MINE: other last-surviving-knights (Sir Lucan dies FIRST; Sir Kay is dead long before Camlann; Sir Gawain is dead), other white-samite arms in lakes (there is only ONE, and it's the same one from Book I -- SYMMETRY), other three-tries scenes (Peter's three denials -- Christian pillar; three-day hunts in Sir Gawain -- Arthurian pillar). Wrong knight: BEDIVERE (not Kay, not Gawain -- Gawain is already dead at Camlann). Wrong sword-fate: THROWN back into the water and CAUGHT by an arm, not buried, not passed to an heir.
history_overlap: None with history. No geography overlap unless a specific lake is named (Malory leaves it unnamed; Dozmary Pool in Cornwall and Loe Pool are both later local claims).

name: The barge to Avalon: the once and future king
scope: Arthur's departure to Avalon, from Malory Book XXI chapter 5-6 (Caxton 1485), Geoffrey of Monmouth (Historia Regum Britanniae Book XI, c.1136), and the epitaph tradition. T1: after Bedivere has thrown Excalibur back into the water, the dying ARTHUR asks to be carried to the shore. Bedivere takes him on his back and brings him down to the waterside. There they find a small BARGE waiting on the water, filled with black-hooded LADIES. T2: THREE (or four in some manuscripts) QUEENS come to the side of the barge and take Arthur aboard, laying him with his head in the lap of one of them. Malory names them: the QUEEN OF NORTH GALES, the QUEEN OF THE WASTELANDS, and MORGAN LE FAY, Arthur's own half-sister -- who had once stolen Excalibur's scabbard but who now weeps over him. With them is NIMUE, the chief Lady of the Lake. Their black hoods and their weeping fill the shore. T3: as the barge draws away Arthur speaks to Bedivere: 'Comfort thyself, and do as well as thou mayest, for in me is no trust for to trust in; for I will into the vale of AVILION (AVALON) to heal me of my grievous wound' (Malory Book XXI ch.5, near-verbatim). The barge moves out onto the water and is lost in mist. Bedivere weeps on the shore. T4: the next morning Bedivere finds a HERMITAGE in a nearby valley where a hermit is digging a fresh GRAVE beside the chapel. Bedivere asks who is buried; the hermit says that at midnight a company of black-hooded ladies came bearing a body which they gave him to bury. Malory refuses to state whether the body is Arthur's or not: 'YET SOME MEN SAY IN MANY PARTS OF ENGLAND THAT KING ARTHUR IS NOT DEAD, BUT HAD BY THE WILL OF OUR LORD JESU INTO ANOTHER PLACE; and men say that HE SHALL COME AGAIN, and he shall win the holy cross. I will not say it shall be so, but rather I will say: HERE IN THIS WORLD HE CHANGED HIS LIFE.' (Book XXI ch.7, near-verbatim, one of the most famous passages in the whole book). T5: on the tomb -- or on the memorial stone at Glastonbury in the story-tradition -- is written the LATIN EPITAPH: 'HIC IACET ARTHURUS, REX QUONDAM REXQUE FUTURUS' -- 'HERE LIES ARTHUR, THE ONCE AND FUTURE KING'. He is not dead but SLEEPS, and will return in the hour of Britain's greatest need. This 'sleeping king who will return' motif runs through the legend and echoes in Wagner's Barbarossa, King Sebastian of Portugal, Ogier the Dane in Kronborg, and Fionn mac Cumhaill sleeping under the hills in Ireland. Further rungs: the name AVALON is Latin Avallo, from Welsh 'Ynys Afallon' meaning 'Isle of Apples' (Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae Book XI); the identification of Avalon with GLASTONBURY (marshland in the west of England, once nearly an island) was made by the monks of Glastonbury Abbey in 1191 when they claimed to have DUG UP Arthur's grave -- a probable pious forgery to draw pilgrims; the 'rex quondam rexque futurus' inscription is Malory's, closing his book; T.H. White's 'The Once and Future King' (1958) draws its title from this line.
source: PRIMARY: Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI chapters 5-7 (the barge, the three or four queens, Morgan le Fay, Arthur's speech about Avalon, the hermitage grave, the 'once and future king' passage). Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book XI (c.1136 -- Arthur carried to Avalon to be healed by Morgan). Geoffrey of Monmouth, Vita Merlini (c.1150 -- Avalon as Isle of Apples ruled by Morgan and her sisters). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Avalon' and 'King Arthur' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Avalon', 'King Arthur', 'Once and Future King', 'Glastonbury Tor', 'Glastonbury Abbey' -- the barge and queens, Morgan le Fay as ferrywoman, the Ynys Afallon etymology (Isle of Apples), the 1191 Glastonbury 'discovery' of Arthur's grave, the 'rex quondam rexque futurus' epitaph. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact wording of the Latin epitaph in Caxton's edition ('rex quondam rexque futurus').
framing_note: The CLOSING ladder of the whole legend. Dinner-test payoffs: T2 (MORGAN LE FAY, who stole the scabbard and tried to kill him, is one of the queens now weeping over Arthur in the barge) and T5 (the epitaph 'here lies Arthur, the once and future king' -- he is not dead but SLEEPS). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the mysterious island where Arthur goes to be healed' AND ask its name; describe the SCENE (a barge on a misty water, black-hooded queens weeping, a dying king laid in a lap, a hermit finding a fresh grave at dawn) and let the recall be the ISLAND (Avalon), the QUEEN (Morgan le Fay), the EPITAPH ('rex quondam rexque futurus'), or the MEANING (he will come again). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Elijah taken up in a chariot of fire (Christian pillar), Baldr laid in his ship-pyre (Norse pillar), Achilles going to the Isles of the Blessed (Greek pillar) -- a hero taken to a mythic place at death, with the possibility of return. Emphasise the sleeping-king motif as a WORLD-MYTHIC pattern (Barbarossa, Fionn mac Cumhaill under the hill, Sebastian of Portugal). DISTRACTOR MINE: other mythic islands (the Isles of the Blessed Greek; Tir na nOg Irish; Hesperides Greek), other black-hooded women (the Fates -- Greek; the Norns -- Norse; the three Marys at the empty tomb -- Christian), other 'sleeping kings' (Barbarossa in the Kyffhauser, Ogier the Dane at Kronborg, Fionn under the hill -- Celtic-Irish pillar). Wrong queen: MORGAN LE FAY (as one of the three queens weeping over Arthur -- she is his HALF-SISTER; despite having been his enemy she is on the barge). Wrong translation: 'REX QUONDAM REXQUE FUTURUS' = 'the once and future king', not 'the king who was and is'. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: Glastonbury Abbey's 1191 'discovery' of Arthur's grave is a REAL historical event -- and almost certainly a pious forgery. State honestly.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the 1191 Glastonbury 'discovery' (the abbey monks claim to find Arthur's grave under the cemetery -- probably a forgery to draw pilgrims after the 1184 fire). GEOGRAPHY owns Glastonbury Tor and Abbey as a Somerset place. Theology owns the STORY of the barge, Avalon, the once-and-future-king inscription.

name: Morgan le Fay: the half-sister who steals the scabbard
scope: Arthur's enchantress half-sister, from Geoffrey of Monmouth's Vita Merlini (c.1150) and Malory Le Morte d'Arthur Book IV chapters 13-14 (Caxton 1485). T1: MORGAN LE FAY -- Old French Morgain la Fee ('Morgan the Fairy') -- is Arthur's HALF-SISTER, one of the three daughters of IGRAINE by Duke GORLOIS of Cornwall (before Igraine's marriage to Uther). She is thus Arthur's elder half-sister; her sisters are MORGAUSE (mother of Gawain and, in Malory, of Mordred) and ELAINE OF GARLOT. T2: Morgan is a SORCERESS -- Geoffrey's Vita Merlini (c.1150) makes her the eldest of NINE MAGICAL SISTERS who rule the ISLE OF AVALON, and she is the wisest, most beautiful, and can HEAL any wound (including Arthur's own eventually). She is educated in a nunnery in Malory and learns 'so much necromancy' there. T3: In Malory Morgan becomes Arthur's ENEMY. She marries King Uriens of Gore against her will; she takes lovers at court; she plots Arthur's death. Her greatest crime is that she STEALS THE MAGIC SCABBARD OF EXCALIBUR -- the scabbard worth ten of the sword whose bearer cannot bleed. She hides it and later (Malory Book IV ch.14), fleeing Arthur's pursuit, she THROWS THE SCABBARD INTO A DEEP LAKE where it is lost forever. From that moment Arthur can bleed and die, and eventually will. T4: Morgan also sends the GREEN KNIGHT (in the shape of Bertilak) to test Camelot in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight -- the poem reveals in Fitt IV that she is the enchantress BEHIND THE ENTIRE beheading game (Cotton Nero A.x). She sends an ENCHANTED CLOAK to Arthur that will burn him to a cinder if he puts it on; Nimue the Lady of the Lake warns him and it burns the messenger instead (Malory Book IV ch.16). She is the villain of a dozen episodes across the cycle. T5: yet at the very end, when Arthur is mortally wounded at Camlann and Bedivere carries him to the barge, MORGAN LE FAY IS ONE OF THE THREE QUEENS ON THE BARGE, and she takes his head into her lap and WEEPS OVER HIM (Malory Book XXI ch.5). Her role reverses: enemy in life, mother-figure at death, carrying him to the Avalon she herself rules to be healed. She is Arthur's most complex antagonist -- kin, sorceress, enemy, ferrywoman, healer -- all in one figure. Further rungs: Geoffrey's Vita Merlini makes her a benign healer-queen of Avalon; Chretien de Troyes and the Vulgate Cycle turn her hostile; Malory blends both -- hostile in life, restorative at death; her name Morgen may derive from Welsh Modron (a mother-goddess); she is often confused with MORGAUSE (mother of Mordred in Malory) -- they are DIFFERENT sisters in Malory though the French tradition sometimes merges them.
source: PRIMARY: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Vita Merlini (c.1150 -- Morgen as chief of nine magical sisters at Avalon; healer of Arthur). Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book I ch.2 (Morgan as one of Igraine's three daughters by Gorlois), Book IV chapters 6-16 (Morgan's enmity: stealing the scabbard, throwing it in the lake, the enchanted cloak, Nimue's warning), Book XXI chapter 5 (Morgan on the barge to Avalon). Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt IV (Morgan revealed as the sender of the Green Knight to test Camelot). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Morgan le Fay' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Morgan le Fay', 'Vita Merlini', 'Avalon', 'Le Morte d'Arthur', 'Sir Gawain and the Green Knight' -- Morgan as Arthur's half-sister and daughter of Igraine and Gorlois, Geoffrey's benign healer version, Malory's hostile version, the scabbard theft, the enchanted cloak, the SGGK role, the barge to Avalon. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether Morgan is the ELDEST or third daughter of Igraine in Malory (Book I ch.2 gives an order).
framing_note: The COMPLEX-ANTAGONIST ladder -- Morgan is Arthur's most layered opponent, and NOT a flat villain. Dinner-test payoffs: T3 (she STEALS THE SCABBARD -- the one thing that keeps Arthur alive -- and throws it into a LAKE) and T5 (at the end she is ONE OF THE THREE QUEENS on the barge that carries him to Avalon, weeping over his head in her lap). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Arthur's sorceress half-sister' AND ask her name; describe the SCENE (a woman educated as a nun and learning necromancy, the scabbard stolen and lost in a lake, an enchanted cloak sent as a gift, a queen weeping on the barge) and let the recall be the SORCERESS, the OBJECT (scabbard), the LAKE, or the BARGE. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Circe the enchantress-queen (Greek pillar), the Morrigan war-goddess-and-woman (Celtic pillar), Freyja who takes half the slain to Folkvangr (Norse pillar) -- a powerful woman who is both dangerous and taking. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Arthurian sorceresses (Nimue/Viviane the Lady of the Lake who WARNS Arthur about Morgan's cloak; Morgause who is Morgan's SISTER and Mordred's mother in Malory -- easily confused), other scabbard-stealers (there is only ONE), other legendary half-siblings-turned-enemies (Loki and the Aesir -- Norse; Cain and Abel -- Christian). Wrong sister: MORGAN LE FAY (the sorceress, scabbard-stealer, cloak-sender, barge-passenger); MORGAUSE (Mordred's mother, wife of King Lot of Orkney) is a DIFFERENT sister. Wrong wife-of: Morgan marries King URIENS of Gore, not Uther, not Lot. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: pure legend.
history_overlap: None with history. GEOGRAPHY owns the general Isle of Avalon question (Glastonbury association).

name: Merlin's end: the enchantress in the rock
scope: The downfall and imprisonment of Merlin, from Malory Le Morte d'Arthur Book IV chapter 1 (Caxton 1485) and the older Vulgate Cycle Merlin and Post-Vulgate Suite du Merlin (c.1230-40). T1: MERLIN in his old age falls in love with a young woman of the LADY OF THE LAKE'S kin -- called NIMUE in Malory (with variants NENIVE, NIVIENE, NIMIANE), VIVIANE in the French Vulgate, and NIMIANE elsewhere. She is beautiful and clever, and Merlin follows her like a lovesick fool wherever she goes. T2: Nimue does NOT love Merlin -- she is afraid of him because he is 'a devil's son' -- but she uses his infatuation. She coaxes his SPELLS out of him one by one, promising she will love him more if he teaches her yet another secret; and Merlin, who FORESAW HIS OWN DOOM but could not prevent it (a mage who knows the future is not free of it), teaches her everything he knows. T3: In Malory the two are travelling in Cornwall when Nimue asks Merlin to show her the wonder under a great STONE. Merlin goes down into the hollow under the stone; and Nimue with the very spells he taught her SEALS THE STONE OVER HIM. Merlin cannot get out. She rides away; the stone stays; and Merlin lies under it forever, ALIVE but trapped, still calling out (Malory Book IV ch.1). T4: variants of the trap differ across the medieval tradition. The FRENCH VULGATE has Nimue enclosing him in a TOWER OF AIR that has no walls but which he cannot cross, in the FOREST OF BROCELIANDE in Brittany. The POST-VULGATE Suite du Merlin has him sealed in a HAWTHORN TREE (the aubepine of Broceliande). In the Welsh tradition Myrddin ends his life mad in the Caledonian forest. All versions agree Merlin does NOT die -- he is IMPRISONED, and can sometimes be HEARD calling out. T5: passing knights in the years after are said to hear his VOICE beneath the stone (or beneath the hawthorn, or from the airless tower), still prophesying, still knowing everything -- but unable to help Arthur when the crisis of Camelot comes. He foresees his own trap and walks into it anyway -- an old, wise, terrible figure undone by the one thing he cannot outsmart, which is his own longing. Nimue after the trap becomes the CHIEF LADY OF THE LAKE in Malory, replacing the earlier lady who gave Excalibur, and she is Arthur's advisor and friend for the rest of his reign -- she warns him of Morgan le Fay's poisoned cloak and rides with him on the barge to Avalon. Further rungs: the earliest Nimue-figure is in the 12th-c. French Estoire de Merlin; Malory's spelling 'Nimue' is idiosyncratic (French tradition prefers Viviane); Broceliande is a real forest in Brittany (the Forest of Paimpont) still visited today for its Merlin associations; Tennyson's 'Merlin and Vivien' in the Idylls of the King (1859) is the Victorian retelling; the fool-mage undone by his own love is one of the great tragic archetypes.
source: PRIMARY: Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book IV chapter 1 (Nimue coaxing Merlin's spells; the trip to Cornwall; the stone; Merlin sealed under it alive). Vulgate Cycle, Estoire de Merlin (c.1215-30 -- Viviane and the Tower of Air in Broceliande). Post-Vulgate Suite du Merlin (c.1230-40 -- the hawthorn tree version). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Merlin' and 'Nimue' and 'Viviane' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Merlin', 'Nimue', 'Viviane', 'Lady of the Lake', 'Broceliande', 'Vulgate Cycle' -- Nimue's coaxing, Merlin's foreknown doom, the stone in Malory, the Tower of Air in the Vulgate, the hawthorn in the Post-Vulgate, Broceliande as Brittany forest, Nimue's later role as chief Lady of the Lake and Arthur's advisor. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether Malory's Book IV ch.1 uses 'stone' or 'cave' (Caxton has 'a great stone').
framing_note: The MENTOR'S DOWNFALL ladder -- Merlin's tragedy is that he FORESAW it. Dinner-test payoffs: T2 (Merlin foresees his own doom and walks into it anyway because a knower of the future cannot escape it) and T3 (Nimue seals him under the stone WITH THE VERY SPELLS HE TAUGHT HER). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the wizard trapped by the enchantress' AND ask which wizard; describe the SCENE (an old mage in love with a young woman, teaching her spells one by one, following her into Cornwall, sealed under a stone) and let the recall be the WIZARD (Merlin), the ENCHANTRESS (Nimue/Viviane), the OBJECT (stone / tower of air / hawthorn -- name the version), or the FOREST (Broceliande). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Odin hanging on Yggdrasil for wisdom (Norse pillar), Samson's hair cut by Delilah (Christian pillar -- a strong man undone by love), or Achilles's heel (Greek pillar) -- a peerless figure undone by his one vulnerability. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Arthurian ladies of the Lake (the FIRST Lady of the Lake who gave Arthur Excalibur -- DIFFERENT figure; Nimue REPLACES her after Merlin's fall in Malory; Morgan le Fay -- also a sorceress but Arthur's SISTER not Merlin's captor), other enchantment-imprisonments (Loki bound under the serpent -- Norse pillar; Prometheus chained to the rock -- Greek pillar; but Merlin is trapped by LOVE and CHOICE, not judgement), other wizards (Gandalf is DERIVATIVE, don't use). Wrong captor: NIMUE (Malory) or VIVIANE (French tradition), NOT Morgan le Fay (Morgan is Arthur's half-sister, not Merlin's love). Name the version.

name: Tristan and Iseult: the love-potion and the sword in the bed
scope: The tragic lovers, from the earliest surviving French verse Tristans (Beroul c.1170, Thomas of Britain c.1175), Gottfried von Strassburg's Middle High German Tristan (c.1210), and Malory Books VIII-XII where 'Sir Tristram of Lyonesse' is folded into the Round Table. T1: TRISTAN (Malory: TRISTRAM; French: Tristan) is a young knight of Lyonesse, nephew and champion of KING MARK OF CORNWALL. King Mark sends Tristan to IRELAND to bring back the Irish princess ISEULT the Fair (Malory: 'Iseult la Beale' or 'Isolde') as Mark's bride. T2: Iseult's mother the queen gives Iseult's maid Brangaine (Brengain in some versions) a LOVE POTION in a golden flask, telling her to serve it to King Mark and Iseult on their wedding night, so they will love each other forever. But on the ship home in the summer heat, THIRSTY, Tristan and Iseult find the flask and drink from it together, thinking it is wine. T3: the potion binds them from that moment. When Iseult marries King Mark, she and Tristan cannot stop loving each other; they meet in secret; their romance runs through the whole Tristan cycle. The great symbol of their divided loyalty is the scene of the SWORD IN THE BED. T4: in the FOREST OF MOROIS, Tristan and Iseult have fled Mark's court together and are living rough in a woodland hut. King Mark, hunting, comes upon their sleeping-place. As he looks in, he sees them lying asleep -- and between them, ON THE BED, TRISTAN'S NAKED SWORD LIES BETWEEN THEIR BODIES like a barrier (Beroul c.1170; Malory Book IX ch.15). Mark, moved by the sight, believes they cannot be lovers (they are, and he is wrong -- but the sword is deliberately placed by Tristan and Iseult exactly to be found this way). He puts his own sword in place of Tristan's as a sign he was there and leaves them unharmed. T5: the story ends in TWO deaths. Tristan, exiled from Cornwall, marries a different woman -- ISEULT OF THE WHITE HANDS (Iseult of Brittany) -- but does not love her. Wounded fighting for her brother, Tristan sends for the ORIGINAL Iseult to heal him. His messenger is to raise WHITE SAILS on the returning ship if Iseult is coming, BLACK SAILS if she has refused. When the ship comes, the wife (jealous of the other Iseult) lies to Tristan and says the sails are BLACK. Tristan dies of grief on the spot. Iseult the Fair steps off the ship, finds Tristan dead, LIES DOWN beside him, and dies of grief also (Thomas of Britain, c.1175; Malory Book XII). Further rungs: the Tristan legend is INDEPENDENT of the Arthurian cycle in origin -- oldest surviving versions are Beroul (Anglo-Norman c.1170) and Thomas of Britain (c.1175), which precede or run parallel to Chretien's Arthurian romances; Malory FOLDS Tristan into the Round Table as 'Sir Tristram of Lyonesse' (Books VIII-XII) but it sits awkwardly there; the WHITE-SAILS / BLACK-SAILS device is directly borrowed from the Greek myth of Theseus's return (Theseus's father Aegeus, mistaking the sails, throws himself off the cliff -- Greek pillar); Wagner's Tristan und Isolde (1865) is Gottfried's version staged and reshaped as opera.

name: Kay the seneschal: the sharp-tongued foster-brother
scope: Sir Kay, from Culhwch and Olwen (Welsh, c.1100), Geoffrey of Monmouth (c.1136), Chretien de Troyes, and Malory Le Morte d'Arthur. T1: SIR KAY -- Welsh Cei, French Ke -- is Arthur's FOSTER-BROTHER, son of SIR ECTOR (Arthur's foster-father) and older than Arthur by a few years. He grew up with Arthur in Ector's household believing they were natural brothers; and when Arthur becomes king he makes Kay his SENECHAL -- the officer in charge of the king's household, feasts, and dining hall. T2: Kay is present at the sword-in-the-stone episode itself: at the New Year's tournament outside London, KAY LEAVES HIS SWORD AT THE INN and sends his young 'brother' Arthur back to fetch it; Arthur finds the inn locked, sees the sword in the stone at the churchyard, and pulls it out to bring to Kay -- who briefly claims to have drawn the sword himself, before Ector forces him to admit the truth (Malory Book I ch.5). T3: Kay's defining trait through the later cycle is his SHARP TONGUE. He mocks other knights, insults strangers who arrive at court, and often chases away real heroes with his taunts -- most famously the young GARETH ('Beaumains', 'Fair-Hands'), Gawain's brother, who comes to court in disguise and is mocked by Kay as a kitchen-boy for a whole year before revealing himself as a great knight (Malory Book VII). In Chretien de Troyes and the Welsh Peredur, Kay similarly mocks the young Perceval when he arrives at court. T4: in the earlier WELSH tradition (Culhwch and Olwen, c.1100), Kay is a MAGICAL WARRIOR: he can hold his breath underwater for NINE days and nights; he can go without sleep for NINE days; his sword-wound never heals; he can make himself as TALL AS THE TALLEST TREE in the forest; the heat of his hand keeps him warm in the coldest weather. He is one of the greatest of Arthur's early warriors -- Bedwyr (Bedivere) and Cei are Arthur's two chief companions in the Welsh tradition, long before Lancelot appears. T5: Malory's Kay is far diminished from the Welsh Cei -- reduced to a stubborn, sharp-tongued, competent-but-not-great household knight, still a member of the Round Table but overshadowed by Lancelot and Gawain and Tristan. He is present at Camelot to the end. In Malory Book XXI Kay's fate is largely off-stage; the Welsh tradition has him killed by Gwyddawg. Further rungs: the Welsh Culhwch and Olwen (c.1100) is one of the OLDEST surviving Arthurian tales, and its Cei-and-Bedwyr pairing is the origin of the later Kay-and-Bedivere pairing; the DEGRADATION of Kay from great Welsh warrior to sharp-tongued seneschal parallels other Welsh figures losing prominence in the French cycle (Bedwyr/Bedivere similar); Kay's mockery of Gareth-in-disguise is one of the great 'don't judge by appearances' stories in Malory.
source: PRIMARY: Culhwch and Olwen (Welsh, c.1100, part of the Mabinogion -- Cei's magical properties: nine days underwater, nine days without sleep, unhealing wound, tall-as-tree). Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book I ch.5 (Kay's forgotten sword at the tournament, Arthur pulling the sword-in-the-stone), Book VII (Gareth/Beaumains and Kay's mockery of him for a year). Chretien de Troyes, Perceval and Lancelot (Kay as sharp-tongued seneschal mocking Perceval and others). framing_note: The FOSTER-BROTHER + DEGRADED-WELSH-HERO ladder. Dinner-test payoffs: T2 (the SWORD-IN-THE-STONE moment happens because KAY FORGOT HIS SWORD at the inn) and T4 (in the OLDER Welsh version he was a magical warrior who could hold his breath for NINE days). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Arthur's foster-brother and seneschal' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a young man leaving his sword at the inn, a sharp-tongued knight mocking a kitchen-boy named Beaumains, a Welsh warrior who can hold his breath nine days) and let the recall be the KNIGHT (Kay), the FOSTER-FATHER (Ector), the CHURCHYARD SWORD, or the WELSH MAGICAL POWER. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Sancho Panza the practical companion (Cervantes, Western pillar), Patroclus to Achilles (Greek pillar), or Enkidu to Gilgamesh (out-of-lane, Mesopotamian) -- a hero's oldest companion, less shining but foundational. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Arthurian companions (Bedivere the one-handed, Lucan the cupbearer, Gawain the nephew), other foster-brothers (there aren't many named), other seneschals (Kay is THE seneschal), the CONFUSION between Kay and Kay's father Ector. Wrong role: seneschal, not marshal or steward or chamberlain. Wrong father: SIR ECTOR (Arthur's foster-father), not King Lot or King Ban.
history_overlap: None with history. Culhwch and Olwen is a real Welsh manuscript in the Mabinogion tradition.

name: Gareth Beaumains: the kitchen-boy who was a king's son
scope: The don't-judge-by-appearances story, from Malory Le Morte d'Arthur Book VII (called 'The Tale of Sir Gareth of Orkney' in Malory). T1: at Pentecost, a tall handsome YOUNG MAN arrives at Camelot without giving his name; he asks Arthur for three gifts -- first, food and shelter for a year with no questions asked; and the other two gifts to be named a year hence. Arthur agrees. T2: SIR KAY the seneschal, mocking the newcomer for his big appetite and his refusal to give his name, DUBS HIM 'BEAUMAINS' -- 'FAIR-HANDS' (Old French) -- and puts him to work in the KITCHEN scrubbing pots. Beaumains works there for a year without complaint, though the other kitchen-boys and Kay mock him constantly. Sir LANCELOT and Sir Gawain, watching, are convinced he is no common man. T3: after his year the young man returns to Arthur and asks his second gift: THE QUEST of a damsel who has just arrived at court, the Lady LYNETTE, who needs a knight to rescue her sister LYONESSE from the RED KNIGHT OF THE RED LAUNDS besieging her castle. Arthur grants it; the young man calls for his horse and armour and rides out with Lynette. All the way to the castle Lynette RIDES BESIDE HIM MOCKING HIM as a kitchen-boy who smells of grease. But at every ford and every bridge Beaumains meets a coloured knight -- the BLACK KNIGHT, the GREEN KNIGHT (a different Green Knight from Sir Gawain's), the RED KNIGHT, the BLUE (INDIGO) KNIGHT -- and DEFEATS each one, sending them back to Arthur as prisoners. Lynette's mockery softens; then turns to admiration. T4: at Castle Perilous he meets the RED KNIGHT OF THE RED LAUNDS -- a giant who has hanged forty knights on trees around his pavilion. They fight all day; at last Beaumains defeats him, spares his life on condition he go to Camelot, and cuts down the forty corpses for burial. T5: at the wedding of Beaumains to Dame Lyonesse (or her sister, depending on manuscript), the young man's identity is revealed: he is SIR GARETH, YOUNGEST SON OF KING LOT OF ORKNEY AND QUEEN MORGAUSE -- Gawain's own YOUNGER BROTHER, and Arthur's own NEPHEW. He had come to court disguised because he wanted to earn his knighthood WITHOUT the advantage of his family name. Gareth is thereafter one of the most beloved of the Round Table. He is also -- with dark foreshadowing -- the KNIGHT WHOSE ACCIDENTAL DEATH at Lancelot's hand during the rescue of Guinevere from the pyre will turn Gawain into Lancelot's mortal enemy and end the fellowship. Further rungs: the Fair-Unknown ('bel inconnu') motif is a whole medieval subgenre -- an unknown hero of noble birth arrives at court in disguise, is mocked, proves himself, and is revealed as a great man's son (Renaut de Beaujeu's 'Le Bel Inconnu' c.1200 is a parallel); Malory's Book VII is one of the most self-contained tales in the Morte d'Arthur, sometimes theorised to be Malory's own composition rather than a translation; Lynette's transformation from mocker to admirer is one of Malory's best character-arcs.

Dinner-test payoffs: T2 (Kay's mocking nickname 'FAIR-HANDS' becomes the knight's whole name for a year of pot-scrubbing) and T4 (a giant Red Knight who has HANGED FORTY knights on trees around his tent, defeated at last).
